html:
Acoustics.

My first real contact with acoustics came when I wrote my master’s thesis, which was on psychoacoustics. There were no Chinese books on the subject then, so I dove straight into Zwicker and Fastl’s Psychoacoustics. I knew very little acoustics and wasn’t used to English textbooks, so it was hard going. But the book isn’t heavy on physics and math; it’s more about perception and statistics, so with a bit of time I could digest it.

Once my PhD started, of course I had to read my advisor’s book: Michael Vorländer’s Auralization. The book is built around auralization, and everything in it serves that goal: source modeling, propagation models and 3D reproduction, the room acoustics, signal processing and 3D playback techniques that go with them, and the fundamentals of acoustics too. Anyone who wants to work on auralization can’t miss it.

Later I got into beamforming, and colleagues recommended the two bibles of microphone arrays: Johnson’s Array Signal Processing and Van Trees’s Optimum Array Processing. The first is easier to follow than the second. Read together, they’ll get you started on arrays, no problem.

I also turn to Acoustics and Room Acoustics by Kuttruff, our institute’s former director, all the time, as reference books on the fundamentals.

For moving sources I mainly read Morse’s Theoretical Acoustics. As the title suggests, the theory is complete and rigorous, and it’s heavy going. But even masters slip up: one of the formulas in the section on moving sources is wrong…

After I started working, I discovered Jacobsen’s Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics and wished I’d found it years earlier. It’s an excellent foundational acoustics book, full of examples and easy to follow, suitable for everyone from beginners to people who have worked in the field for years.

I’ve just bought Gonghuan Du’s Fundamentals of Acoustics and Jianchun Cheng’s Principles of Acoustics (2nd edition, two volumes), both in Chinese. I haven’t read them closely yet, only leafed through them, but my impression is that Fundamentals of Acoustics compares with Jacobsen’s book and is easier to get into, while Principles of Acoustics compares with Theoretical Acoustics and takes real effort.
